1. REFRAME: You have already spent money and time on equipment and games; those costs are gone and cannot be recovered by continuing. The actual decision is whether to spend future time and money on activities that do not generate enjoyment, justified only by the false logic that past spending creates present obligation. The pattern across sports and games suggests you are confusing sunk costs with reasons to act.

2. STAKES: You stand to lose hours of life spent in low-enjoyment activities, plus additional money on equipment maintenance or in-game purchases, weighed against the discomfort of admitting a past decision was wrong. Anyone who depends on your participation in these activities (teammates, gaming friends, family members who support your involvement) stands to lose your presence. You also stand to gain back discretionary time and money for pursuits that actually interest you, and to break a decision-making pattern that is clearly harming your welfare.

3. CONSEQUENCES: If you continue playing: You will spend future time in activities ranked low on your own enjoyment scale; you will likely spend additional money to maintain participation; the sunk-cost reasoning will strengthen, making it harder to quit later; and you will model to yourself the principle that past mistakes justify present suffering. If you stop: You will experience acute discomfort from admitting the purchase was wasteful (moderate probability of 2–4 weeks of regret); you will have 5–15 hours per week freed immediately; teammates or gaming communities may express disappointment (moderate probability, low duration); and you will face the temptation to fill the freed time with another sunk-cost trap (moderate-to-high probability of recurring behavior unless you address the underlying pattern).

4. RECOMMENDATION: Stop both activities now and do not replace them with similar spending patterns. The money is already lost—continuing is not recovery, it is loss extension. Yes, this is uncomfortable: you must absorb the fact that you made a bad judgment, and you will feel it acutely. That discomfort is the price of correcting course, and it is far smaller than the cost of years spent in joyless obligation. Some people may feel let down; that is their problem, not a claim on your time. The deeper issue is your decision-making process: you are vulnerable to the sunk-cost fallacy and to reward loops designed to extract money. Before filling the freed time, identify what you actually want to do, not what you feel obligated to do. Therefore: quit now, sit with the discomfort of the wasted expense for a few weeks, and use the reclaimed time to build the habit of choosing activities for their intrinsic reward rather than their cost history.
